text: The Vikings sailed far from home. They voyaged as far as the Mediterranean, North Africa, the Middle East, Greenland, and Vinland, in present-day Newfoundland.
The Vikings were the first Europeans to reach North America. They briefly settled in Newfoundland, which they called Vinland.
Longships were long, slender ships built for speed. They could carry a large crew of warriors.
Leif Erikson bought a ship from Bjarni and gathered a crew of thirty-five men. Then he set off to find the lands Bjarni had described.
Erik the Red, the father of Leif Erikson, founded the first Norse settlement in Greenland. Leif was raised there.
After wintering in Vinland, Leif returned to Greenland in the spring. He brought back a cargo of grapes and timber.
A castle was a fortified building made in the Middle Ages. It was built mostly by nobles or royalty, and by military orders.
Castles took many forms in the Middle Ages. Some parts, such as curtain walls, arrowslits and portcullises, were common.
Between 1066 and 1087, King William set up 36 castles, such as Warwick Castle. He used them to guard against rebellion in the English Midlands.
Knights were mounted warriors. Often a knight was a vassal who served a lord as an elite fighter or a bodyguard. His payment was land.
By about 1420, complete suits of plate armor had been developed in Europe.
Armorers fitted armor to the person who would wear it, like a tailor. They made parts that needed to bend from smaller individual plates called lames.
The Silk Road got its name from the valuable trade in silk, which was first developed in China.
The name Silk Road was made popular in 1877 by Ferdinand von Richthofen. He made seven expeditions to China from 1868 to 1872.
Marco Polo traveled widely inside China. He lived in the emperor's lands for 17 years and saw many things that Europeans had never known.
In 1269, Niccolò and Maffeo Polo came home to Venice and met young Marco for the first time. By then Marco was 21 years old.
The Bactrian camel is the largest mammal in its native range. At the top of the humps, its average height is 6.99 ft (213 cm).
A thirsty camel in a hot, dry season can drink up to 53 US gallons (200 L) of water in one day.
The Great Wall of China is a series of fortifications in China. They were built across the northern borders of ancient Chinese states, to protect against nomadic groups.
The Great Wall had watchtowers, troop barracks and garrison stations. It could send signals with smoke or fire.
The three pits of the Terracotta Army hold more than 8,000 soldiers. There are also 130 chariots with 520 horses, and 150 cavalry horses.
The Terracotta Army figures vary in height according to their rank. The tallest are the generals.
The Song dynasty was the first government to issue paper currency.
A Song dynasty book describes a magnetic navigation device. It was an iron south-pointing fish floating in a bowl of water.
Leonardo da Vinci was a painter. He also kept notebooks. In them he drew and wrote about the body, the stars, plants and maps.
Leonardo painted the Mona Lisa. It is regarded as the world's most famous painting. His Last Supper is the most reproduced religious painting.
Leonardo became an apprentice by the age of 17. He remained in training for seven years.
Two of Michelangelo's best-known works, the Pietà and David, were sculpted before he was 30.
Michelangelo did not think of himself as a painter. Still, he painted scenes from Genesis on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome, and The Last Judgment on its altar wall.
Galileo built a telescope. He saw the stars of the Milky Way, the phases of Venus and the four largest moons of Jupiter. He also saw Saturn's rings and sunspots.
The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain around 1760. By about 1840 it had spread to Europe and the United States.
The textile industry was the first to use modern production methods. Textiles became the main industry in jobs, in value of output and in money invested.
Mechanized cotton spinning was powered by water and later by steam. It increased output per worker by a factor of around 500.
In 1712, Thomas Newcomen built an engine that sold well. It could give steady power to a machine.
James Watt saw that engines of his day wasted a lot of energy. They cooled and reheated the cylinder again and again. His separate condenser avoided this waste.
James Watt developed the idea of horsepower. The unit of power called the watt is named after him.
At its peak, Mali was the largest empire in West Africa. It spread its language, laws and customs across the region.
About two thirds of the gold that moved around the Mediterranean in medieval times came from West Africa. That was almost half of the Old World's gold.
Mansa Musa made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca from 1324 to 1326. He gave away so much gold that prices went up in Egypt.
After the visit by Mansa Musa around 1325, Timbuktu flourished. Its trade in salt, gold and ivory made it rich.
In its golden age, Timbuktu had a big book trade. It also had a university, the Sankoré Madrasah.
The Great Enclosure at Great Zimbabwe has walls as high as 36 ft (11 m). They extend about 820 ft (250 m).
